title: Build features that belong in Wuff
markdown:
# Build features that belong in Wuff

New products are Empire modules. Read [Product modules](/docs/modules) for source
ownership, contribution points and the Todo/Totake reference implementations.

This is Wuff's implementation guide for contributors and their coding agents.
You describe the behavior and try the result. Your agent handles the code, Git,
checks and PR. You can build and iterate independently; Tim reviews and merges.

## Start with your idea

Use the starter prompt above in your authorized repository workspace. Explain the
problem, who benefits and what should become easier. Your agent should offer
small product choices, show the main interaction early and keep a short record of
agreed decisions. You do not need to choose libraries or manage Git yourself.

Describe → write a brief → implement → try the preview →
refine → verify → Tim reviews → Tim merges/releases.

Start at [Build a feature](/docs/build), then use [Review and delivery](/docs/review)
when the result is ready. Read the product rules, design language, real component
reference and accessibility requirements while building.

Read [API, MCP and connections](/docs/surfaces) before defining the feature. Every
persisted-data action needs API/MCP capability parity, an MCP UI decision and a
connection/consent/revocation review; keep these current as the feature develops.

## Which instructions do what?

| Layer                                       | Job                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Root and nearby AGENTS.md                   | Repository entry point, architecture boundaries and links to the workflow             |
| This implementation guide                   | Product rules, real components, design decisions and quality requirements             |
| wuff-contributor skill                      | Walk the agent through discovery, independent iteration, verification and PR delivery |
| GitHub policy, permissions and owner review | Check delivery evidence and control what can reach main                               |

Your current checkout is authoritative. Hosted documentation and downloads may lag
unmerged changes. A skill helps the agent follow the rules; it cannot grant tools,
credentials, hosting or permission to bypass them.

## Your workspace must be ready

Use your own GitHub account and a workspace supplied or approved by Tim. Do not
borrow his credentials, copy production data or test writes on an unverified
preview. A Vercel preview URL does not prove database isolation. The build guide
lists the setup gates; if something is missing, your agent prepares a concrete
technical handoff and can explore a clearly labeled local mock while waiting.

## What to share with your agent

- Your goal, intended users and examples of the current problem.
- Screenshots or sketches you choose to share, plus feedback on early iterations.
- The intended Wuff task if this work is already tracked.
- Which parts of the idea are essential and which can wait.

The guide is public and its component examples use synthetic data. Reading it
never grants access to your private lists or production services. There is one
contributor workflow; the separate prototype kit and design-handoff skill are retired.

title: What Wuff does today
markdown:
# What Wuff does today

New products are Empire modules. Read [Product modules](/docs/modules) for source
ownership, contribution points and the Todo/Totake reference implementations.

Empire Settings has its own navigation, independent of Todo. Personal Your apps
and Dashboard choices control app launchers and summaries. Hiding keeps data,
notifications and connections; AI access needs explicit app/service permissions.
AI clients and notification devices/status are global; Todo owns its schedules,
GitHub and Cursor settings. Global and per-app pauses are enforced by the delivery callbacks. Totake owns its medication/equipment repeat and recording rules. Real installed notification delivery remains a release gate.

Wuff Empire is the shared web portal at `/`, with an app menu and a personal
dashboard. Wuff Todo stays at `/lists`; Wuff Totake opens its private medication/equipment workspace. Its optional portal summary shows counts and reminder-group links without medicine names. Todo previews reuse authorized Todo reads.
App navigation never grants access to another person's private information or
expands an existing connection's permissions. Web Todo's Overview is the existing
Home view; MCP keeps Home. The portal and Todo startup preferences are
separate: opening `/` always opens the portal.

Wuff Todo helps friends and family manage private and shared lists. It also has an optional Work mode for development tasks. Keep everyday lists fast and approachable; richer features should not make every simple task feel like project management.

## Lists and tasks

- Private lists or shared lists with accepted editors; personal sidebar order.
- List descriptions, seven owner-selected colors, sections, archive/restore.
- Tasks with inline names, explicit completion/reopening, shared manual ordering and one level of subtasks. Children have independent completion; deleting a parent also deletes its children.
- Rich notes stored as Markdown, private note images, explicit Save/Cancel and retained drafts when a save fails or remote content changes.
- Optional calendar due dates, including Today/Tomorrow/custom/clear. A date is not a shared due time. Completing a task removes urgency styling; reopening appends it to the active order.
- Personal views: filtering, grouping, sorting, density and collapsed groups. These do not change someone else’s view or shared manual order. Dragging is unavailable under computed sorting.
- Optional Work lists: Todo, In progress, In review, Blocked, Done; priority, one assignee, external references, stable task links and WUFF keys.

## Permissions are part of the design

| Action                                      | Owner                      | Accepted editor | Non-member     |
| ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | --------------- | -------------- |
| Read tasks and notes                        | Yes                        | Yes             | No             |
| Add/edit/complete/delete/reorder tasks      | Yes                        | Yes             | No             |
| Rename/delete/archive list                  | Yes                        | No              | No             |
| Change shared metadata, colors and sections | Yes                        | No              | No             |
| Invite or remove people                     | Yes                        | No              | No             |
| Move a task to an existing section          | Yes                        | Yes             | No             |
| Change own view and reminder preferences    | Yes                        | Yes             | No             |
| Leave the shared list                       | Ownership must be resolved | Yes             | Not applicable |

Access is invite-only. Existing admitted people accept account-bound invitations before seeing tasks; a URL or email does not grant access. Reader-only membership, ownership transfer and public self-registration are not current features.

## Collaboration and integrations

Open screens refresh after list changes, including changes through MCP. Remote updates must preserve unsaved input and offer recovery from conflicts. Failed or uncertain saves never look confirmed.

GitHub linking and issue synchronization exist for owner-authorized repositories. Personal Cursor connections and agent controls exist, but paid execution has a separate operational gate. Shared-list membership never grants someone else’s credentials or credits.

Personal reminders and Settings are implemented. Scheduling, delivery-provider configuration and installed-device notification delivery are separate capabilities: a saved preference is not evidence that a notification can be delivered. Reminder times and daily inclusion are personal; they are not shared task due times.

## Surfaces and boundaries

The responsive website and MCP tools use the same authorized backend; the MCP App adds an embedded interface. Installable PWAs use the responsive web application. Tauri/native apps are retired. Browser checks do not prove physical-device push delivery or a named MCP-host integration.

No offline list cache or queued offline edits. No arbitrary palette colors, dark mode, recurring tasks, multi-level subtasks or new admission model by default. These can be proposed as new scope, with their implications explained rather than presented as already supported.

Preserve these defaults unless the feature deliberately changes them. Explain proposed product changes in the PR; admission, access and privacy changes need explicit review in the PR before merge. Contributors can prepare and test code without preliminary approval.

## Current interaction language

Saved views are personal to each list. Save view updates the current view; Save as
new view creates a named view. Shared list settings separate List details, People,
Only for me and Manage list. Home completion and task-title navigation are separate.
Date shortcuts and Clear date change a draft; Save date commits it.

In Settings → AI & MCP connections, each MCP client has app/service switches and
an advanced individual tool list. These choices only narrow the existing OAuth
grant and are separate from menu visibility. Connection controls stay available
when authorized. AI clients can turn tools off; the owner re-enables them in
Settings. After saving, refresh the client tool catalog; cached disabled calls
are blocked immediately. Newly added optional tools stay off after a selection.

title: Build a Wuff Empire module
markdown:
# Build a Wuff Empire module

A product is a module inside the existing monorepo and deployment. Todo, Totake and
Notes are the reference implementations. Start with the nearest module rather
than copying an entire app or adding a plugin loader.

## Ownership and entry points

| Layer                    | Product-owned source                                                | Empire responsibility                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Manifest and tool policy | `packages/contracts/src/modules/<id>/manifest.ts`, `mcp-catalog.ts` | Client-safe installed registry in `packages/contracts/src/modules.ts`; validates IDs, routes, widgets, groups and tools |
| Contracts and rules      | `packages/contracts/src/modules/<id>/`                              | Actor/error/ID, account, notification and design contracts in `platform/`                                               |
| Database                 | `packages/db/src/modules/<id>/schema.ts`                            | `schema.ts` composes tables; one migration chain and connection                                                         |
| Domain                   | `packages/domain/src/modules/<id>/`                                 | Shared admission, transactions, notification delivery and settings orchestration in `platform/`                         |
| Shared web/MCP UI     | `packages/ui/src/modules/<id>/`                                     | UI primitives, account-pinned API and platform runtime                                                                  |
| Website                  | `apps/web/src/modules/<id>/pages`, `api`, `web`                     | Thin Next route entry points preserve public URLs and framework configuration                                           |
| MCP                      | Product `mcp.ts` and `mcp-app.ts`                                   | Transport, authenticated actor, scope/tool filtering, resource packaging and shared embedded controls                   |
| Dashboard                | Product `dashboard.tsx`                                             | Layout and choice filtering; typed UI registry in `apps/web/src/modules/ui.ts`                                          |

The public `@wuff/contracts` and `@wuff/domain` barrels remain compatibility
surfaces. New module adapters should use explicit product subpaths where practical.
Do not move server code into a client-safe registry. Shared UI must not import the
server registry or database package. Product UI imports real `@wuff/ui` primitives.

## Add a product

1. Choose a stable lowercase ID and routes. Add its manifest, schemas and tool
   policy. Declare navigation, settings links, dashboard widget IDs/defaults,
   approved theme, permission labels and tool groups. Registration rejects
   duplicate ownership and reserved routes. Module tools cannot become mandatory
   platform controls or request undeclared scopes. For a deliberate cross-product
   capability, declare `integrations: [{ moduleId: "todo", scopes: ["lists:read",
"tasks:write"] }]` as Notes does for task creation. Registry validation checks
   the target owns those permissions. This declaration does not grant scopes;
   the actor still needs explicit OAuth consent and destination access.
2. Add the product to `packages/contracts/src/modules.ts`. Register actual UI
   components in `apps/web/src/modules/ui.ts` and server MCP registration in
   `apps/web/src/modules/server.ts`. The typed registries require an entry for
   every installed product. The manifest contains no React or database imports.
3. Implement authorized domain operations and product-owned tables. Export schema
   definitions through the shared database composition entry point. Keep the single
   Drizzle migration history; no migrations on page load or on an app switch.
   Schema changes need their normal migration review and execution authorization.
4. Add thin filesystem routes for Next.js and preserve explicit framework exports.
   Settings panels belong to the product; the global navigation discovers their
   manifest links. Implement HTTP adapters and MCP tools against the same
   authorized domain services. Native/Tauri clients are retired; do not add native
   registrations or adapters. Register embedded renderers in
   `modules/mcp-ui.ts` when an
   interactive MCP view is appropriate; complete tools remain available without it.
5. If the product schedules notifications, contribute reconciliation and scheduling
   through `packages/domain/src/platform/module-services.ts`. Product code owns
   repeat rules/content and job tables; the platform owns devices, transport and
   global pause/privacy. Extend persisted per-app pause storage/contracts with a
   reviewed migration when adding a new notification-producing app; current
   columns are intentionally still Todo/Totake. Check pause, resume, stale callback
   and device isolation. Shared services must not invent medicine or task actions.
6. Run registry, unit, HTTP/MCP and relevant browser checks. Record explicit
   consent/revocation and MCP UI decisions under the surface contract. Update this
   guide when an extension point changes, and keep the feature PR current.

## User choices are independent

Show app controls launcher/navigation visibility. Dashboard controls its widgets.
Tool choices narrow each MCP connection's actual OAuth grant. Notification pauses
are enforced on the server. None implies another. Hidden apps retain authorized
direct links, data and reminder delivery; settings remain reachable for recovery.
There is no new destructive uninstall or activate/deactivate lifecycle in this
refactor. A later deactivation capability must define background-work and data
retention behavior and expose equivalent authorized API/MCP operations.

New optional tools stay off after an explicit tool selection. Enabling a module
never broadens consent, refresh permissions or provider access. Module registrars
receive an ownership-filtered context; current scope checks and disabled cached
calls remain the platform's responsibility. Never register tools directly on the
raw server to bypass that boundary.

## Design and compatibility

Use the shared design tokens, controls, full-width layouts, fonts and accessibility
rules. The manifest records an approved default palette; existing Todo list-owned
themes still take precedence inside Todo. Adding a manifest is not a license to
replace global CSS or invent arbitrary theme colors. Preserve module-local design
choices, including Totake's screens and recording workflow.

Native clients are retired; new modules need web/PWA and HTTP/MCP capabilities.
Cross-product
features call a deliberate platform orchestrator or public service, never reach
into another product's private UI or data internals.

## Notes as a new-product example

Notes adds `/notes`, `/settings/notes`, an opt-in `notes.summary` widget and twelve
MCP tools. Its manifest is `packages/contracts/src/modules/notes/manifest.ts`;
the adjacent catalog declares actual tool permissions. Notes owns eight additive
tables under `packages/db/src/modules/notes/`, using the same account and migration
chain. Domain services in `packages/domain/src/modules/notes/` enforce private
ownership, direct Viewer/Editor membership, versioned edits, personal pin/archive
and operation receipts before any adapter returns content.

Its Todo integration calls Todo's authorized transaction service to create a task
and source reference atomically. It does not copy Todo implementation, access list
tables to bypass its service, or share linked notes implicitly. Shared private-image
normalization/storage lives in `domain/src/platform/image-storage.ts`; reads remain
owned by the product's access boundary. See [Notes scope and evidence](../wuff-notes.md).

When adding a product read scope, update and test both consent validation and the
OAuth server's scope validation. Keep omitted-scope defaults and existing refresh
grants unchanged. A manifest does not itself authorize new scopes. Retired native
identities and resources must remain denied.

title: Wuff’s visual language
markdown:
# Wuff’s visual language

Wuff is calm, compact and warm. Waffles is a small companion, not a corporate mascot. Keep tasks and readable controls in charge. Use the live palette selector on this guide to see the same color derivation used by the product.

## Use the actual tokens

Import `listPalette` and `listThemeVariables` from `@wuff/design`, or render `ListTheme` from the shared UI. The selected list drives the full experience: page, sidebar, surfaces, controls, text and focus. Settings drafts do not silently save or preview a new list color. Auth and contexts with no selected list use Blue.

| Palette | Primary accent | Reference tint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blue | #315f9b | #eaf1fb |
| Lavender | #7355a3 | #f1ecf9 |
| Sage | #34705a | #e9f4ee |
| Rose | #a23f66 | #fbeef3 |
| Peach | #a5502c | #fcf0e9 |
| Sand | #826619 | #f8f3e3 |
| Slate | #526779 | #edf1f5 |

The reference tint is a palette entry, not a substitute for derived page or surface values. The ten CSS roles are `--wuff-primary`, `--wuff-primary-hover`, `--wuff-background`, `--wuff-surface`, `--wuff-sidebar`, `--wuff-accent`, `--wuff-foreground`, `--wuff-muted`, `--wuff-border`, and `--wuff-control`. Use their semantic Tailwind names (`bg-background`, `bg-surface`, `text-foreground`, `text-muted-foreground`, `border-input`, `outline-primary`). Subtle separators and interactive control boundaries are deliberately different colors.

Semantic status colors stay recognizable across list palettes: review violet, blocked/danger red, done green. Reuse StatusTag and shared CSS rather than deriving these from the list accent.

## Type, spacing and shape

DM Sans is used for headings, body text and controls, with real italic font files for notes. Code is monospace. Use the bundled fonts and license; do not fetch a different family from a CDN.

Shared buttons use a 44px minimum height, 8px radius, 14px/20px semibold labels and 8px internal gaps. Inputs/selects are 44px high, text-base and rounded-md; textareas grow with content. Status tags are compact, non-interactive text/icon badges. These are actual component defaults, not permission to shrink touch targets.

Favor small, purposeful gaps (4/8/12/16/24px) and quiet borders. Keep the task’s completion, name and actions aligned. Current TaskRow CSS has completion and trailing actions at 44px around flexible content, without a permanent empty drag gutter. Read the source when extending a row; historical screenshots may predate its latest layout.

## Actions and feedback

| Intent                        | Existing treatment                                         |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Primary/add/save              | Button variant primary; filled list accent, explicit label |
| Secondary/cancel              | default or outline; bordered surface                       |
| Quiet utility                 | ghost; named icon or concise words                         |
| Destructive utility           | danger; quiet red                                          |
| Confirm irreversible deletion | destructive; filled red with explicit consequence          |

A new shadcn component is a proposal until integrated. Do not run shadcn init or replace Wuff’s controls with stock shadcn styling. Wuff does not ship every upstream primitive: for example, it uses a native select and several feature-owned dialogs/disclosures rather than a universal Select/Dialog library.

## Voice

Labels such as Save notes, Cancel, Delete list and Allow connection stay literal. A short friendly dog joke can appear in surrounding guidance: “No tasks to fetch,” or “A little more de-tail.” Avoid stacking jokes and never hide failures, permissions or destructive consequences. Keep user-written titles and notes unchanged.

title: Real components, visible behavior
markdown:
# Real components, visible behavior

These demos import Wuff’s shipped React components. The inventory below is generated
directly from exported declarations in `packages/ui/src`. Use its exact signatures
and inspect event behavior in the current repository source; do not substitute
upstream shadcn defaults or a copied component tree.

Use the component search and jump links to find a component by name or source path. Expand a module for its exact props.

## The primitive layer

| Module                 | Exports and API notes                                                                                              |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| @wuff/ui/button        | Button: primary, default, outline, ghost, danger, destructive; default/sm/icon sizes; asChild; native button props |
| @wuff/ui/input         | Input: native input props, invalid/disabled/focus styling                                                          |
| @wuff/ui/textarea      | Textarea: native textarea props and shared styling                                                                 |
| @wuff/ui/native-select | NativeSelect: native select props/options; inset decorative chevron                                                |
| @wuff/ui/input-group   | InputGroup, InputGroupAddon, InputGroupButton, InputGroupText, InputGroupInput, InputGroupTextarea                 |
| @wuff/ui/status-tag    | StatusTag: status todo, in_progress, in_review, blocked or done; a label, not a button                             |

InputGroupAddon supports inline-start/end and block-start/end. InputGroupButton exposes xs/sm/icon-xs/icon-sm; use icon-sm or another 44px target for touch actions. The existence of a compact size is not an accessibility guarantee for a new use.

## Feature components

TaskRow, task metadata, notes/editor, due-date controls, task actions, task groups/detail drawer, ListSettings, Sharing, ListApp, personal views, Work metadata, GitHub/agent controls, reminders, sortable controls, Corgi and ListTheme are included. Some depend on FeatureRuntime, parent callbacks, task/list shapes and live state. Use their declared props; do not treat them as isolated zero-configuration primitives.

The interactive TaskRow example uses synthetic data, in-memory changes and an
injected runtime. Unsupported actions explain that they are not simulated; the
guide never contacts private services. This is a component reference, not a
standalone application or proof of backend behavior.

## Source and reuse

`packages/ui/src/features/runtime.ts` defines FeatureRuntime and RuntimeContext.
It separates shared components from routing, requests and account
behavior. `@wuff/contracts` supplies public types; `@wuff/design` supplies palette
derivation; `@wuff/client` supplies the browser-safe live-refresh queue. Real features use the existing
authorized runtime/adapters. Database and domain packages stay server-side.

Inspect import paths and signatures, then read the matching repository file for
event behavior and other types. `pnpm build:guide` refreshes the inventory directly
from source. Download hashes identify the published guide resources, not a copied
app. The current checkout governs any difference from the hosted snapshot.

title: Responsive and accessible by design
markdown:
# Responsive and accessible by design

Design the feature so it is usable on a phone and with a keyboard from the first working iteration. Existing components provide useful defaults; each new composition still needs review.

## Viewports and content

- Inspect 320px and 390px phone widths, plus desktop around 1280px. Add intermediate widths when the layout changes. Long names, long links and expanded editors must fit without horizontal document scrolling.
- Keep compact task rows readable. Collapse secondary actions where appropriate, with visible labels when expanded. Preserve direct completion and recognizable primary actions. Mobile navigation must remain reachable.
- Let text wrap and containers shrink (`min-width: 0`); avoid fixed widths for main content. Horizontal code/table examples may scroll inside their own labelled region.
- Check both Compact and Comfortable density when changing rows. Test empty, one-item and crowded lists, subtasks, completed tasks, archived/read-only screens and different palettes.

## Input, keyboard and focus

- Target at least 44×44 CSS px for common touch actions. All icon-only controls need accessible names; decorative icons are hidden from assistive technology.
- Use real buttons, labelled inputs, native selects and native disclosure semantics. Placeholder text does not replace a label. Avoid nested interactive controls.
- Keep focus visible. Inline rename supports Enter to save and Escape to cancel; closing an editor or dialog restores focus to the trigger. A modal needs an accessible name, focus management and keyboard dismissal where appropriate.
- Reordering needs a non-drag alternative. Existing sortable controls support keyboard operation and position picking; touch scrolling must remain usable. Sorted/filtered views cannot reorder the shared list incorrectly.
- Explain validation beside its field, use aria-invalid/aria-describedby when needed, announce status without stealing focus, and do not announce every keystroke.

## State and consequences

Show loading, pending/saving, saved, empty, offline/request-failure, denied, stale/conflicting and disabled states where relevant. A failed save retains the draft and provides a clear recovery action. A local mock or component example must distinguish simulated results from actual persistence.

Deletion has explicit confirmation and names affected subtasks/members when relevant. The cancellation path preserves data. Personal preferences must be labelled as personal rather than implying a change for the whole shared list.

## Color, motion and review limits

Text and controls must remain understandable without color. Use semantic text/icons alongside state colors. Aim for WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text and meaningful controls/focus boundaries), checking new combinations against their actual background. Preserve reduced-motion behavior; animation must not be required to understand or operate the feature.

Review keyboard sequence and focus in the rendered implementation, not only its JSX. Browser viewport checks do not prove a physical device, touch keyboard, screen reader or full accessibility conformance. State which checks were performed and leave untested behavior explicit.

Reference: [W3C guidance on text contrast](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html).

title: API, MCP and connections are core product surfaces
markdown:
# API, MCP and connections are core product surfaces

Wuff is an app and an agent-accessible service. A feature is incomplete when it
changes persisted data only through the website. Every contributor must design and
verify its API, MCP and connection behavior before calling the feature complete.

## Every mutation has equivalent capabilities

For each create/update/delete/reorder/archive action, personal preference or other
persisted data change, identify the shared server-side domain operation, authorized
HTTP API route and MCP tool. Reuse an existing route/tool when its contract already
supports the action; a new feature does not always require a new endpoint name.
Include authorized reads so an agent can discover the current state and verify a
write. Update shared contracts, client adapters, tool schemas/descriptions and
returned snapshots together. No business logic or permission checks belong only
in a page handler, React component or MCP adapter.

API and MCP use the same domain services, actor/access rules, validation, defaults,
personal/shared semantics, version conflicts, operation IDs and retry behavior.
Both must return enough authorized state to reconcile success or recover from an
uncertain save. Existing web/PWA views must refresh after MCP writes and MCP
reads must reflect API writes. Preserve pending drafts during remote refresh.

No web-only mutations, placeholder tools or silent API/MCP deferral. If backend
scope or credentials are unavailable, keep a clearly labeled draft/mock and hand
Tim the required technical changes. Do not ship the feature as complete.

## Decide whether it needs an MCP App UI

Consider extending the existing MCP App when the feature benefits from browsing,
selecting, editing structured content or inspecting state visually. Reuse the
shared design/components and authorized tools. A small atomic tool action may
need no new UI; explain that decision in the brief.

The PR declares either implemented UI with verification, or not-needed with a
reason. Required UI cannot be silently deferred. Tool-only usage must remain
complete in clients that cannot render an MCP App. Respect host sandbox/resource
policies, never embed secrets, and distinguish protocol/local SDK proof from an
actual named host's interactive behavior.

## Treat connections as part of the feature

Review both delegated Wuff AI-client connections and external provider connections
such as GitHub/Cursor. Declare affected connection types, required scopes, explicit
consent, setup/status/disconnect behavior and any secure browser handoff. Reuse
existing connection management; do not create a parallel token store or silently
add scopes to existing grants. Refreshes cannot expand authorization.

Missing, expired, revoked or insufficient-scope connections need explicit recovery
without falsely reporting success. Revocation must take effect on the next access
and on retries/replayed receipts. A shared list never grants another person's
credentials, provider consent or paid execution rights. Secrets remain server-side
and never appear in MCP output, client bundles, logs or screenshots.

API/MCP equivalents expose authorized capabilities and status, never raw tokens
or privileged internal callbacks. Use the existing browser consent/sign-in handoff
when secrets or provider policy require it, with an agent-usable status/recovery
path. Call out new scopes or changes to consent/auth for Tim's review before merge;
preparing and testing code does not require preliminary approval.

## Evidence required before review

For each mutation, show an API write followed by an MCP read and an MCP write
followed by an API/web read against isolated synthetic data. Exercise relevant
owner/editor/outsider access, personal-state isolation, invalid input, duplicate
operation IDs, stale versions and concurrent writes. Confirm defaults and returned
state match across adapters. New adapter coverage must call the actual adapters;
mocking their responses does not prove parity.

For affected connections, cover absent/expired/revoked grants, missing scopes,
explicit consent recovery, disconnect, cross-account privacy and retries after
revocation. For MCP UI, exercise its actual controls and tool-only fallback, state
which host/runtime was tested, and refresh the tool catalogue after schema changes.
Builds and JSON declarations alone never prove this behavior.

## Record the surface contract in every PR

Describe persisted operations with their shared domain function, authorized HTTP
route, MCP tool and actual adapter verification. Explain the MCP App UI decision
and connection/scope/consent/revocation impact. For changes with no persisted-data
behavior, explain why these surfaces are unaffected.

Keep this proportional and current as implementation evolves. Plain language or a
table is sufficient; no JSON schema or metadata check is required. Drafts may
contain planned operations, but implementation and verification must be complete
before claiming delivery. Copilot/Codex review comments help identify omissions;
reviewers still inspect actual code and adapter evidence.

title: Build a feature
markdown:
# Build a feature

New products are Empire modules. Read [Product modules](/docs/modules) for source
ownership, contribution points and the Todo/Totake reference implementations.

Work in the actual Wuff repository, using its components, contracts and authorized
services. You choose the behavior; your agent manages implementation and delivery.

## Give your agent this starter

> Use the wuff-contributor skill. Read AGENTS.md and docs/contributor-workflow.md in
> this repository, plus the product, design, component and accessibility guide.
> Help me define the problem, behavior and acceptance criteria. Create a codex/
> branch and draft PR. Build and iterate independently without waiting for Tim
> to approve briefs, file lists or routine technical choices.
> Reuse Wuff's actual components and tokens, show the main interaction early, and
> iterate with me. Preserve permissions, personal/shared boundaries and save recovery.
> Map every persisted mutation to API and MCP equivalents, assess MCP UI and
> preserve connection scopes, consent and revocation. Add meaningful unit tests for changed behavior and regression tests for fixes. Handle Git and verification for me. Use synthetic data and only a confirmed
> isolated preview backend. Call out access/privacy, schema, permissions and
> safeguard changes for final review; production operations, migration execution
> and paid runs need Tim's explicit authorization. Keep decisions, current-commit evidence and remaining
> gaps in the PR. Do not merge or release. My idea is:

## One workflow, including exploration

Sketching, small local mocks and visual experiments are useful steps inside the
feature's draft PR. They do not become a separate app, a replacement component
system or evidence of real persistence. Clearly label simulations and connect the
actual behavior through existing services as the feature develops.

The full contributor workflow follows and is also available as a download above.


## Build a Wuff feature safely

This workflow covers real feature work in the repository. The contributor chooses
product behavior and tries the result. Their agent handles Git, code, checks and
the PR. Contributors build and iterate independently; Tim and Josibe84 may merge their own PRs after required checks and the Codex fix/review loop. Agents still need explicit instructions to merge. A draft PR may be
incomplete; ready for review requires the evidence below.

### Before the first feature

Tim must finish these gates before granting contributor write access:

- Activate and verify main protection with PRs, resolved threads, Verify (`check`). This is one-time onboarding, not per-feature approval.
  Current activation evidence and remaining onboarding limits are recorded in
  [GitHub safeguards](https://github.com/timbenniks/wuff-todo/blob/main/docs/contributor-github.md).
- Give each person their own GitHub credentials and no administration or bypass
  access. Never lend Tim's gh login, production credentials or environment files.
  Prefer upstream read access plus a private fork, where the repository's plan and
  fork settings allow it. They push their feature branch to their fork and open
  a PR to upstream main. Upstream write access also permits changing branch
  workflows and emitting similarly named Actions checks; required owner review
  remains essential. Check names alone are not an adversarial security boundary.
- Supply a disposable workspace with synthetic data. A branch/worktree does not
  isolate commands or secrets. Use a dedicated container/account or hosted
  environment without production credentials, privileged MCP connectors or access
  to Tim's credential files. Repository instructions are not a sandbox.
- Confirm preview database, auth and Blob isolation, restrict preview access and
  disable real notifications, paid agent runs and provider side effects. Do not
  test preview writes until Tim confirms this setup; a Vercel URL proves no data
  isolation.

Repository changes do not provision a contributor sandbox or preview backend.
Until those gates pass, use read-only access or clearly labeled local mock work
inside the feature branch. There is no separate standalone prototype workflow.

### 1. Understand and define

Read root/nearby AGENTS.md, implementation plan, product spec, architecture,
development, verification and relevant feature docs. Read the product, design and
accessibility guide. Inspect existing code before inventing another component,
service or dependency.

Create one `codex/` branch and early draft PR using the repository template. Never
reset another person's edits, force push shared work or rebase someone else's
branch. Fetch main and resolve conflicts on the feature branch; ask for technical
help if the correct behavior is unclear.

Keep the brief proportional to the change; a small fix needs only a few sentences.
Implementation can start immediately in the ready workspace. Fill `## Feature brief` with the problem, intended users, included/excluded
behavior, existing behavior to preserve and testable acceptance checkboxes. Under
`## Scope`, identify files, UI/API interactions and sensitive changes. Resolve
product questions with the contributor in ordinary language. Do not ask them to
choose database designs or approve infrastructure commands.

Use `docs/guide/` (hosted at `/docs`) for product, design, component and accessibility
rules. Show the main interaction early, offer small concrete product choices and
keep a short decision log. Distinguish preserved behavior from proposed changes.
Record entry points, outcomes, cancellation/recovery and personal/shared effects
so the brief stands alone without the chat. Local mocks are an iteration tool,
not proof of backend persistence or authorization.

Complete `## API, MCP and connections` using `docs/guide/surfaces.md` as the
implementation develops and before requesting final review. Inventory every persisted mutation and its shared domain/API/MCP mapping,
authorized reads, MCP UI decision and connection/consent/revocation impact. Existing
tools may be extended; web-only data changes cannot be marked complete.

### 2. Build and iterate independently

No preliminary approval from Tim is required for a brief, file list, implementation
choice or ordinary feature iteration. There are no scope hashes, path allowlists
or line-count approval thresholds. Contributors and their agents can edit UI,
styles, domain services, API/MCP adapters, contracts, dependencies and tests as the
feature requires. Keep the brief current when the intended behavior changes.
Ask the contributor product questions when needed; do not route routine technical
decisions through Tim. Show the main interaction early and incorporate feedback.

Call out changes to admission, authorization, sharing/privacy rules, OAuth consent,
schema/migrations, production configuration and safeguards in
the PR. You can prepare and test these changes in the isolated workspace without
preliminary permission; reviewers assess their implications before merge. Path-based
policy hints draw attention to likely risk and never replace semantic review.
Do not disable protections or weaken tests to make a feature pass.

Operational authorization is separate from writing code. Explicit authorization
from Tim is required to execute migrations, provision/change infrastructure,
deploy to production, publish releases, run paid agents or perform destructive
operations on real accounts/data. Do not use production credentials or Tim's
personal credentials. Ordinary source edits, synthetic fixture cleanup and local
build/cache operations in the ready workspace do not need extra permission.

If an operation or environment is unavailable, continue useful implementation,
unit tests or clearly labeled mocks and record the concrete handoff. Do not turn
an operational blocker into a blanket stop on feature development.

### Product module ownership

Read [the module guide](guide/modules.md) before adding or changing a product.
The brief names its owning module and platform contributions. Todo and Totake own
contracts, domain, schema, UI and adapters; Empire composes typed registrations.
New modules use this structure, shared authentication/design/transport and the
same API/MCP contract. Keep settings visibility, dashboard preferences, MCP consent
and notification delivery separate. Do not copy the app or add runtime plugins.

### 3. Implement within Wuff's boundaries

- Reuse components, tokens, typography and interactions from `@wuff/ui`. Preserve
  compact layouts, 44px grouped action targets, keyboard/focus and accessible
  labels. Do not initialize a replacement component system.
- Keep server/domain/database code out of browser bundles. Use existing authorized
  services. Every persisted-data feature ships equivalent API and MCP capabilities
  through the same domain operations. Assess MCP App UI and connection handling
  explicitly; do not postpone parity until a later feature.
- Preserve private admission, owner-only list administration, shared editor
  permissions, personal preferences/credentials and online-only behavior. Use no
  real private data in previews.
- Preserve version checks, operation IDs and exact-payload retries. Handle stale
  writes and uncertain saves without duplicate mutations or silently losing drafts.
- Avoid unbounded reads, per-row repeated requests, eager heavy editors and
  duplicate subscriptions. Measure query/request or bundle impact when affected.
- Explain dependencies, contract changes and global styling changes in the PR.
  Highlight the high-risk changes listed above for final review. Routine
  implementation choices and evolving file lists do not require permission.
- Add meaningful regression coverage for changed permissions, retries, concurrency
  and recovery. Do not weaken tests, hide errors with suppressions, mock away the
  tested behavior or change safeguards just to get a green check.
- Keep one feature per PR, record decisions/evidence in its feature document, and
  report unrelated defects separately instead of expanding scope.

The policy conservatively flags sensitive files. It cannot identify every risky
code path or judge architecture; Tim must inspect semantic changes too.

### 4. Verify and record current evidence

Every new or changed behavior requires meaningful unit coverage: successful
outcomes, boundary/invalid inputs and applicable failure/recovery cases. Bug fixes
need regression cases that fail without the fix. Test observable contracts, not
private details, static copy, CSS classes, source text or stubbed success.

`pnpm test` automatically discovers nested JS/TS unit files under `tests/` and
excludes `*.integration.test.*`. Adding a unit test must not require editing a
manual list. Python helper behavior also needs the appropriate local test command.
Line coverage or a test count alone is not proof of meaningful behavior coverage.

Describe changed unit test files, meaningful cases, commands and actual results
in the PR. Integration checks do not replace unit coverage. Docs/style-only
changes may explain why no testable behavior changes; persisted-data changes
cannot waive coverage. No machine-readable JSON declaration is required.

Run `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test` and relevant integration/UI checks. Keep the PR a
draft when required checks are blocked/unrun and never claim completion from a
build alone. Write a meaningful failing case first when practical. Use the
configured isolated backend and synthetic accounts for integration tests. Never
fall back to production when local services are unavailable.

For UI changes, exercise 320px, 390px and desktop, long content, keyboard/focus,
labels, relevant palettes and applicable loading/empty/error/denied/conflict
states. Check overflow, cancellation, retries and preserved drafts. Attach
screenshots and reproduction steps. Browser checks do not prove screen-reader or
physical-device behavior; report only accessibility checks actually performed.

For server changes, verify relevant owner/editor/outsider isolation,
revocation, idempotency, concurrent/stale writes and API/MCP parity. Record actual
performance measurements when affected. Native compilation and installed-platform
checks are Tim's local release gate; Vercel's web build is separate evidence.

For each persisted mutation, prove API-write/MCP-read and MCP-write/API-or-web-read
against isolated data, including relevant permission/conflict/retry failures. For
affected connections, test missing/expired/revoked grants, insufficient scopes,
explicit consent recovery, disconnect and cross-account credential privacy. MCP
UI needs actual control checks and tool-only fallback; report the host tested.

Record verification commands/results and identify the source commit tested in
the PR. No exact `Evidence commit:` string or synchronized full-head SHA is
required by a metadata gate.

After new code, rerun affected checks and update evidence; do not just relabel old
results with a new SHA. Under `## Preview`, link the deployment for that commit,
test steps and who confirmed backend isolation. If unavailable, explain the
blocker and local evidence. Never invent a preview or isolation claim.

### Resolve review findings

After pushing a feature, have the existing Codex reviewer inspect the latest head.
Use the configured automatic review; if none runs, request `@codex review` on that
feature PR. A draft may need an explicit request. Do not mark work ready merely to
trigger a review while checks are blocked. Review usage has its own availability;
do not purchase credits, add a paid service or bypass a limit without Tim.

1. Read Codex's summary, inline findings and human review threads. Record the
   reviewed commit SHA and link. An older review does not cover later code changes.
2. Fix each actionable bug, add its regression coverage, run relevant checks and
   push the fix. Reply on its thread with the fix commit and actual evidence;
   when this workflow is invoked for delivery, these review requests/fix replies
   on the feature PR are part of the requested work. Never publish credentials or
   private user data in comments.
3. For a disputed finding, explain the code path and evidence; leave it visible
   for Tim's decision. Do not blindly implement incorrect advice, count a resolved
   thread as proof of a fix, or close/dismiss someone else's unresolved objection.
4. Request a fresh Codex review after fixes, wait for completion and inspect new
   findings. Repeat for newly introduced bugs. If review is unavailable or the same
   dispute persists, keep the PR draft and give Tim a concrete handoff instead of
   sending repeated review requests or pretending it passed.
5. Fill the PR's Review findings section with the current reviewed SHA/link,
   addressed findings/fix commits/tests and remaining issues. If code has changed
   since that review, state this explicitly. Only report no outstanding findings
   after checking the latest summary and threads. Tim resolves disputed findings
   and owns final review/merge; bot suggestions and unrelated comments are not all
   automatic blockers.

Codex review is independent of `pnpm` tests, application builds, integration/device
proof. Its no-findings result does not prove those checks
ran, that the review was exhaustive or that merging is technically prevented.
As of October 26, main is protected by the active public-repository ruleset and
hosted Verify runs; the metadata policy was retired on October 28. Inspect the latest head's actual
results; a prior green run does not cover a new push. If required hosted checks
become unavailable, run meaningful local checks and retain the honest blocked/draft
status. The GitHub ruleset supplies enforcement; these instructions/templates do
not independently lock merging. See [current enforcement](contributor-github.md),
[activation evidence](public-safeguards-activation.md) and
[the review-loop scope](pr-review-loop.md).

### 5. Submit for review

Review the entire diff for unintended files, secrets, debug data and regressions.
Match acceptance criteria to observed behavior. Fill `## Remaining work or risks`
with gaps, consequences, rollout steps and responsible people; explain when no
known risks remain. Mark ready only when checks pass and evidence is sufficient.
The PR template and Copilot/Codex comments guide delivery descriptions; actual
tests and review establish evidence. There is no contributor metadata gate.

Give the contributor a plain-language summary, PR/preview links and remaining
technical help. Do not merge, push main, deploy or mark the feature released. Tim
reviews UI, architecture, evidence and rollout before merging and can request
changes even when automated checks pass.

### Technical help without blocking the idea

When operational authorization or infrastructure is missing, prepare a concrete handoff: user goal,
proposed technical change, affected files, risks and smallest alternative. Keep
the draft PR/mock reviewable. Never ask a nontechnical contributor to authorize
migrations or production commands.

### Supported clients

Web, PWA and MCP only. Do not require native adapters/builds or register Tauri
clients. [Native retirement](native-retirement.md) records the removed product
and deliberate legacy authorization/transport rejection. Browser-native HTML
controls and shared web UI remain supported.

title: Review and deliver a feature
markdown:
# Review and deliver a feature

Keep one clear record of the agreed behavior, implementation and evidence in the
PR. The conversation supports that record; Tim should not need to reconstruct it.

## Before asking for review

- Match the final behavior to the brief and observable acceptance criteria. Keep
  exclusions, preserved behavior, permission rules and personal/shared effects explicit.
- Link the exact preview deployment and source commit. Confirm Tim can open it.
  Include simple test steps and annotated phone/desktop screenshots where useful.
- Record the existing components/services reused, intentional visual departures,
  high-risk changes and important technical decisions in feature docs.
- Report applicable success, loading, pending, empty, error, denied and conflict
  behavior, including cancellation, retained drafts and uncertain-save recovery.
- List commands actually run, results, mocked behavior, unverified checks and
  rollout/device gates. A green check is not proof that evidence is true.
- Include meaningful unit cases for all changed behavior, regression tests for
  fixes and the PR's Unit tests section. Verify new tests are discovered by
  `pnpm test`; integration-only coverage or empty assertions do not substitute.
- For every data-changing operation, include shared domain/API/MCP mappings and
  actual cross-surface adapter evidence. Record the MCP App UI decision and
  affected connection scopes, consent, recovery, revocation and privacy checks.
  Web-only writes and unresolved parity work cannot be presented as complete.

Keep the brief current when the contributor changes direction. Do not turn
unanswered questions into requirements; ask product questions when needed.
After new code, rerun affected checks and update the evidence for the current PR
head. Tim can request changes even when every automated check is green.

## Keep Wuff tracking useful

If the contributor asks to create/update a Wuff task, resolve the intended Work
list and check for an existing task first. Read current state/version, preserve
existing notes/attachments, use a fresh operation ID for a new mutation and verify
its result. Do not guess a list or upload images without the user's intent.

Use Todo for scoped work ready to start, In progress while implementing, In review
when submitted and Blocked for a concrete dependency. Do not mark Done or claim
release until the agreed acceptance/release gates are met. A PR, preview and Wuff
task each have a different purpose; label their links clearly.

Without connected Wuff tools, provide a ready-to-paste update. A task write never
by itself authorizes paid agent execution, a migration, merge or production release.

## What the contributor receives

Give a plain-language description of what changed, how to try it, what was tested
and any remaining gates. Tim and Josibe84 may merge their own PRs after required
checks and the Codex fix/review loop. Agents need explicit merge instructions;
production operations still need Tim’s authorization.

## Module review

Confirm product code lives in its module and shell changes use typed contributions.
Check route/tool ownership, schema identities, module registration failures and
client bundles. New products need real UI/server/notification adapters, deliberate
MCP App UI and consent decisions, and the same surface verification as existing apps.
